---
order: 2
unit: water-australia
title: "Why does water run short?"
node: AC9HG7K02 n2
summary: "Water scarcity means not having enough usable water. This lesson sorts its causes three ways: too little water in the place, water that is there but cannot reach people, and more water being used than the place can supply. It also looks at why the amount of water changes: seasons, evaporation, location and the shape of the land."
language: maths
hook: "A town has a river running right past it, yet its taps keep running dry. How can that be?"
---
**Water scarcity** means people do not have enough usable water for what they need. Geographers often sort its causes three ways. It is a way of sorting, not a law: real places often have more than one cause at once.

- **Physical cause**: there is not enough water in the place. Little rain falls, or water evaporates fast.
- **Economic cause**: the water is there, but people cannot get it because the pipes, pumps, dams or treatment needed have not been built or have broken down.
- **The ways water is used**: more water is taken, by farms, industry or towns, than the place can supply.

**Variability** means how much the amount of water changes from season to season and year to year.

## Predict: a river and dry taps

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Commit to a reason before learning that 'not enough water' has more than one cause."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Made-up Corrowin has a river beside it all year, but its taps often run dry. What is the most likely reason?"
  options:
    - "The town has no working way to get the river water to its houses"
    - "It must not be raining enough at Corrowin to fill the taps"
    - "The river must be too small to supply a whole town"
    - "People in Corrowin must be wasting too much water"
  actual: "The water is there. What is missing is a way to get it, clean, into people's houses: pumps, pipes and treatment. That is an economic cause, not a lack of rain."
```

## Try: sort the causes

```step
stage: run
insight: "Sorting causes three ways shows that 'not enough water' can mean different problems."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "In these made-up cases, what is the main cause of the shortage?"
  options: ["Physical cause", "Economic cause", "The ways water is used"]
  items:
    - ["Very little rain falls for years at a time", "Physical cause", "There is not enough water in the place."]
    - ["Hot sun and wind dry up water stored in open dams", "Physical cause", "Evaporation takes the water away."]
    - ["The town cannot afford to build a plant to clean its river water", "Economic cause", "The water is there, but the town cannot make it fit to use."]
    - ["Old pipes leak and break, so water does not reach the houses", "Economic cause", "The problem is the system that delivers the water."]
    - ["Farms upstream take more water from the river every year", "The ways water is used", "Demand has grown faster than the supply."]
    - ["A new factory uses a large share of the town's water", "The ways water is used", "Another use competes for the same water."]
```

Was your prediction right? "Not enough water" and "not enough rain" are different things.

## Worked example: two dry towns

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Ask two questions in order: is the water physically there, and can people reliably get usable water?"
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Made-up Drybank has had little rain for three years, and its dam is nearly empty. What kind of cause is this?"
      options:
        - "Physical: there is not enough water in the place"
        - "Economic: the town has the wrong pipes"
        - "The ways water is used: the town uses too much"
        - "Economic: Drybank's dam must be too small"
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - "That blames the pipes, but pipes cannot deliver water that is not there. The rain stopped."
        - "Use could make it worse, but the case says the rain stopped."
        - "A bigger dam cannot fill without rain and runoff, and both have stopped."
      explain: "The water itself is missing, so it is a physical cause."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#nib"
      text: "Nib is explaining Corrowin. Click the first line where Nib's thinking goes wrong."
      answer: 4
      fault: logic
      misconception: scarcity-always-means-no-rain
      explain: "Line 4: the river is there all year, so the water is physically there. The taps run dry because the town cannot get the water to its houses. Nib's fix in line 5, a dam to catch rain, would not help."
    smaller:
      check:
        type: question
        q: "In made-up Corrowin the river is full, but the pump to the houses is broken. What is missing?"
        options: ["A way to get the water to people", "Water in the river"]
        answer: 0
        feedback: [null, "That assumes the shortage is in the river, but the river is full. The break is between the river and the houses."]
        explain: "The water is there. What is missing is the way to deliver it."
    hint:
      - "Line 2 says where the water is."
      - "Find the line that guesses a cause the case does not support."
      - "Is the river short of water, or are the houses?"
```

### Two questions in order

```worked
\text{Is the water physically there?} :: Drybank, no: little rain for years. That is a physical cause.
\text{Can people reliably get usable water?} :: Corrowin, no: the river is full, but pumps, pipes or treatment are missing. That is an economic cause.
\text{Is more being taken than the place can supply?} :: If farms or a factory take more each year, that is a cause from the ways water is used.
\text{Why it matters} :: Each cause needs a different fix. A dam does not help Corrowin; new pipes do not help Drybank.
```

### Find Nib's slip

## Vary: why the amount changes

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Variability factors explain why the amount of water in a place changes, and each works in its own way."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: match
      q: "Match each factor to how it changes the water in a place."
      pairs:
        - - "Seasonality"
          - "Most rain falls in one part of the year, so rivers run high then low"
        - - "Evaporation"
          - "Heat and wind turn stored water into vapour"
        - - "Topography"
          - "The shape of the land decides where water runs and collects"
        - - "Location"
          - "In Australia the driest areas are inland, far from the coast"
      explain: "Each factor changes how much water there is, or when. Name the factor and say how it works."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "In northern Australia almost all rain falls in the wet season, from about November to April (Bureau of Meteorology). What does this mean for a river there?"
      options:
        - "It can run high in the wet season and low or dry for the rest of the year"
        - "It carries about the same amount of water every month, whatever the season"
        - "It has the most water in the dry season, when the weather is hottest"
        - "Seasons only change the groundwater under it, not the river on the surface"
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - "Rivers fill from rain. If the rain comes in a few months, so does most of the flow."
        - "Heat in the dry season speeds up evaporation, so there is less, not more."
        - "Rivers fill from rain and runoff, so seasons change them directly."
      explain: "That is seasonality: the amount of water changes through the year."
```

## Practise: name the cause

```step
stage: practise
insight: "The diagnosis decides the fix, so name the cause before choosing a response."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Made-up Corrowin fixes its pipes and pumps. Then a long dry spell leaves its river very low. What kind of cause is it now?"
      options:
        - "Physical: now the water itself is short"
        - "Economic: the pipes must have broken again"
        - "Economic: if the pipes are fixed, it must be the pumps now"
        - "The ways water is used: Corrowin must be wasting water"
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - "The case says the pipes were fixed. What changed is the river."
        - "That sticks with the first diagnosis. The evidence changed: the river itself is low."
        - "The case does not say use went up. It says the rain stopped."
      explain: "The same town can have different causes at different times. Diagnose from the evidence."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Old pipes at made-up Corrowin leak, so river water does not reach the houses. Which response targets that cause?"
      options:
        - "Repair or replace the pipes"
        - "Build a bigger dam to catch more rain"
        - "Ask people to wait for wetter years"
        - "Ask everyone in Corrowin to use less water"
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - "More stored water still has to travel through the same leaking pipes."
        - "Rain is not the problem here, so waiting does not fix it."
        - "Using less does not help if the water never reaches the houses."
      explain: "An economic cause needs a fix to the system that delivers the water."
```

### Match the fix to the cause

## Make: two towns, two causes

```step
stage: make
insight: "Explaining a physical and an economic cause in your own words shows the difference is yours."
check: { type: reflect, text: "In my own book I explained one physical cause (Drybank) and one economic cause (Corrowin) of water running short, and two factors that make the amount of water vary, saying how each one works. A partner gave feedback." }
```

Both towns are made up. Write it in your own book or document, not on this page. Use the two questions: is the water there, and can people get it?

## Typical: more than one cause

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "Real shortages often combine causes. Name each one."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "A made-up town has dry years, a growing population and a treatment plant that is too small. Sort each fact by the cause it shows."
  options: ["Physical cause", "Economic cause", "The ways water is used"]
  items:
    - ["Less rain falls in dry years", "Physical cause", "There is less water in the place."]
    - ["The treatment plant cannot clean enough water", "Economic cause", "The water could be there, but the system cannot make enough fit to use."]
    - ["More people move in each year and use more water", "The ways water is used", "Demand is growing."]
```

## Wider: same cause, same fix?

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
insight: "Comparing places tests whether one fix suits different causes."
check: { type: reflect, text: "With a partner I compared a made-up place short of rain with a made-up place that has water but no pipes or treatment, and explained why the same strategy would not suit both." }
```

Typical and wider steps are extras on the same idea. You do not need them to finish the lesson.

```teacher
summary: "Students sort the causes of water scarcity three ways (a physical
  shortage, an economic cause where water is there but cannot be delivered or
  treated, and the ways water is used) and explain factors that make water vary:
  climate, seasonality, evaporation, location and topography. This is the second
  hinge: mixing up physical and economic causes leads to mismatched strategies
  in lesson 4."
learning: distinguish physical and economic causes of water scarcity and explain
  factors that make water resources vary
time: 40
timing: Predict and Try 7 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary 7 min · Practise 6
  min · Make 8 min. Typical and wider steps are extras.
goals:
  - I can tell a physical cause of water scarcity from an economic one.
  - I can name a cause that comes from the ways water is used.
  - I can explain how two factors, such as seasons and evaporation, change the
    water in a place.
struggle: "Students collapse every shortage into 'not enough rain'. Ask the two
  questions in order, out loud, every time: is the water physically there? Can
  people reliably get usable water?"
before: >
  This is the second hinge (K02 n2). The node's reason: confusing physical and
  economic causes leads students to recommend engineering fixes for economic
  scarcity, or the reverse, in node 4. Protect the Corrowin bug task and its
  smaller step.


  The three causes are ACARA's elaboration (physical, economic, the ways water
  is used). They are a way of sorting causes, not a law, and the lesson says so;
  real places often have more than one, which the typical step shows. "Economic"
  here means the water is there but people cannot get it because infrastructure
  is missing, broken or unaffordable; some students hear "economic" as "about
  money" only, so name pipes, pumps and treatment.


  Drybank and Corrowin are made up, with made-up conditions. They are not meant
  to stand for any real Australian town. The one real fact used is the northern
  wet season (almost all rain from about November to April; Bureau of
  Meteorology, ABS Year Book Australia 2005). The location factor says only what
  the source supports: the driest areas are in the interior (same source). No
  climate-change or ENSO claims are made; ENSO is a node wider item for teachers
  who want it, with historical records from the Bureau of Meteorology.
running:
  - "Predict: take a vote. Most students pick 'no rain'. Let that sit until Try."
  - "Try: stop after the pipes item and ask: is the water there? Can people get
    it?"
  - "Worked example: say the two questions aloud before the bug task. Protect
    the smaller step for students who stall."
  - "Vary: ask for 'how it works', not just the factor's name."
  - "Make: check each cause is named with its town, and each factor with how it
    works."
stuck:
  - see: Every shortage is put down to low rainfall.
    ask: Is the water physically there? If yes, what stops people getting it?
    fix: "Separate the water from the delivery: river, then pumps, pipes and
      treatment, then taps."
  - see: "'Economic' is read as 'the town is poor' only."
    ask: What would the town need to build or fix to get the water to people?
    fix: Economic causes are about the system that delivers water (dams, pipes,
      pumps, treatment) not being there or working.
  - see: A factor is named but not explained.
    ask: How does seasonality change the water? When is there more, when less?
    fix: Name it, then say how it changes the amount or the timing.
support: "Give the two questions on a card: 'Is the water physically there?' and
  'Can people reliably get usable water?'"
stretch: Explain how population growth and a run of dry years together could
  make a shortage worse than either alone. Same level, more width.
leads: >
  Next in Water in Australia: what water distribution means for people in
  different places.


  First Nations content: none of ACARA's elaborations for AC9HG7K02 names a
  First Nations example; this lesson has none. Any local example should come
  from community-approved material.


  ACARA elaborations used here: "identifying the causes of variability in water
  resources or water scarcity; for example, an absolute shortage of water
  (physical cause), inadequate development of water resources (economic cause),
  or the ways water is used (such as farming, industry, drinking, washing or
  watering)" and "explaining the factors that contribute to variability in water
  resources or water scarcity; for example, location, climate, topography,
  seasonality or evaporation".
exit:
  q: Give one physical and one economic cause of water running short, and say why
    the same fix would not suit both.
  a: "Physical: little rain for years, so the water is not there. Economic: the
    water is there but pipes or treatment are missing. A dam does not fix
    missing pipes, and new pipes do not make it rain."
explain: >
  **Water scarcity** means not enough usable water for what people need. One way
  to sort its causes:


  - **Physical**: not enough water in the place (little rain, high evaporation).

  - **Economic**: the water is there, but pipes, pumps or treatment to get it to
  people are missing.

  - **The ways water is used**: more is taken than the place can supply.


  **Variability** factors (seasons, evaporation, location, the shape of the
  land, climate) change how much water there is and when.
sources:
  - title: Australia's climate (Bureau of Meteorology chapter, ABS Year Book
      Australia 2005)
    url: https://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/0/35F9CDF3307C036ECA256F7200832F12
    checked: 2026-11-01
class:
  inquiry:
    q: A town is short of water. Should it build a new dam?
    prompts:
      - What would you need to know first?
      - When would a dam not help at all?
    notes: "Steer to diagnosis before a fix: is the water physically there, and can
      people get it? This is the move lesson 4 builds on."
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: discussion
      title: River, but dry taps
      minutes: 3
      do: Read the Corrowin hook. Vote on a reason, then hold the answer until Try.
      notes: Most students will say 'no rain'. Leave it; the sort and the bug task
        turn it round.
    - at: investigate
      kind: discussion
      title: Two questions in order
      minutes: 5
      do: Pairs apply the two questions to Drybank, then Corrowin, before the bug
        task.
      notes: "Protect the hinge: students who cannot separate 'there' from 'reachable'
        will mismatch strategies later."
    - at: make
      kind: activity
      title: Swap and check
      minutes: 6
      do: Students write their two causes and two factors in their books, swap, and
        the partner checks each cause is named and each factor says how it
        works.
      notes: The reflect tick records completion. A partner or the teacher reads the
        writing; the site does not mark it.
```
